name: Teaching Large Language Models to Self-Debug
authors: Xinyun Chen, Maxwell Lin, Nathanael Schärli, Denny Zhou (Google DeepMind; UC Berkeley)
reflection_type: verbal-self-critique combined with tool-verified feedback. The model performs 'rubber duck debugging' by explaining its own generated code in natural language (self-critique), and where unit tests are available it incorporates code execution / unit-test execution results as external tool-verified feedback. Four feedback formats: Simple (correctness only), UT (unit-test execution results), +Expl (code explanation), +Trace (model-generated execution trace).
feedback_source: Hybrid. (1) self-generated: model-produced code explanation and execution-trace explanation; the model itself infers correctness when no tests exist (e.g. Spider text-to-SQL). (2) external-tool/unit-tests: code execution via an interpreter and unit-test pass/fail + runtime error messages when available (TransCoder, MBPP). No human feedback and no ground-truth error messages are used.
iteration_structure: iterative-refine. One turn = Generation -> Explanation -> Feedback; the feedback message (explanation + execution results) is appended and fed back to the model for further turns. Debugging stops when feedback says the prediction is correct or a maximum of 10 turns is reached; empirically successful debugging mostly ends within 3 turns (one turn usually sufficient on Spider, additional turns add <0.1%).
reflection_object: output content — specifically the model's own generated program (SQL query, translated Python code, or text-to-Python code). The model reflects on and rewrites the code; the natural-language code explanation / execution trace is an intermediate reasoning artifact used to localize the bug, but the modified object is the predicted program itself. No reasoning-chain, weights, prompt, or skill library is modified.
requires_training: none — pure few-shot prompting at inference time; the pretrained LLM is used without any fine-tuning or weight update.
reward_or_critic_model: self-as-judge plus verifiable reward. The model acts as its own critic by explaining the code and predicting correctness; when unit tests are present, deterministic unit-test execution provides a verifiable reward signal. No trained reward model or separate critic model is used.
distillation_target: none — reflection is not distilled into any persistent reusable artifact; it is transient within the debugging session of a single problem. No memory, skill, rule, prompt-update, or weight is produced.
emergent_vs_engineered: prompt/scaffold-engineered. The reflective rubber-duck-debugging behavior is elicited by hand-designed few-shot demonstrations and a fixed Generation/Explanation/Feedback prompting pipeline, not RL-emergent. There is no 'aha'-style emergent reflection from training.
memory_type: short-term/scratchpad — the running feedback transcript (prior code, explanations, execution results, prior revisions) is accumulated within the prompt context across debugging turns for a single problem. No long-term or cross-task memory store.
memory_persistence: within-episode — the accumulated feedback/explanation context persists only across the debugging turns of one problem instance and is discarded between problems; nothing carries across tasks or sessions.
memory_curation_mechanism: append-only — within a debugging episode, each turn's explanation and execution feedback is appended to the prompt context; there is no summarization, eviction, or selection mechanism, and the transcript is bounded only by the max-10-turn limit (typically <=3 turns in practice).
error_localization_granularity: block-level (code) / response-level. The model explains the code line-by-line and compares it to the problem spec to localize discrepancies (e.g. a missing WHERE condition or wrong SELECT column), then revises the whole program. Localization is at the level of code lines/segments within the generated program rather than token-level or multi-agent-level.
intra_task_vs_inter_task: intra-task — refinement happens within a single problem (iterative debugging of one program). There is no transfer of experience across different tasks/problems (unlike Reflexion/ExpeL/AWM).
failure_recovery_vs_avoidance: post-hoc-revision — the model first produces a full candidate program, then detects and corrects errors after generation by explaining and (optionally) executing it, iterating until correct. It is not mid-trajectory in-flight recovery and not next-episode avoidance.
task_domains: code generation across three sub-domains: text-to-SQL generation (no unit tests), code translation (C++-to-Python), and text-to-Python generation. Broadly: code.
benchmarks: Spider (text-to-SQL, dev set, no unit tests), TransCoder (C++-to-Python translation, 560 problems with 10 unit tests each), MBPP (500 text-to-Python problems, 3 unit tests each with 1 shown in prompt).
headline_result: On Spider (no unit tests), Self-Debugging with code explanation improves the baseline by 2-3% consistently and by ~9% on the hardest (extra-hard) problems (e.g. Codex 77.5 -> 80.8; with multi-sample baseline 81.3 -> 84.1). On TransCoder and MBPP (unit tests available), Self-Debugging improves baseline accuracy by up to 12% (e.g. Codex TransCoder 80.4 -> 92.5 with +Expl; GPT-4 TransCoder 77.3 -> 90.4; GPT-4 MBPP 72.8 -> ~80.6). It also matches/outperforms baselines that sample >10x more candidate programs.
baselines: Greedy-decoding single-sample baseline and multi-sample execution-based selection baseline; prompting-only rerankers MBR-Exec (Shi et al. 2022) and Coder-Reviewer (Zhang et al. 2022); trained-verifier/finetuned methods LEVER (Ni et al. 2023) and T5-3B + N-best Reranking (Zeng et al. 2022); and an 'oracle baseline' that resamples a new program (with access to all unit tests) whenever greedy decoding is wrong.
gains_vs_baseline: Spider (Codex): baseline 77.5 -> +Expl 80.8 (+3.3); multi-sample baseline 81.3(n=32) -> 84.1, beating LEVER 81.9(n=50) and T5-3B+N-best 80.6(n=25). TransCoder (Codex): 80.4 -> 92.5 (+12.1) with UT+Expl; oracle baseline only 84.5. MBPP (Codex): 61.4 -> 70.8 with +Trace; multi-sample 72.2(n=10) -> 75.6 beating LEVER 68.9(n=100). GPT-4 gains: TransCoder +13.1 (77.3->90.4), MBPP +~8 (72.8->80.6). StarCoder MBPP +6 (47.2->53.2). Self-Debugging exceeds the resample-oracle baseline, showing repair beats discard-and-resample.
compute_cost_profile: Inference-time only (no training). Each debugging turn adds extra LLM calls (one explanation generation + one revised-code generation) and code executions, plus growing context; capped at 10 turns but typically <=3, with most gains in turn 1. Net effect is a small per-problem inference multiplier that is far cheaper than the alternative: it matches or beats execution-selection baselines that sample >10x more candidate programs, i.e. it improves sample efficiency rather than increasing total cost.
known_limitations: Performance is ultimately bounded by the underlying LLM's capability (large room for improvement remains). Does not scale to large real-world codebases where bugs emerge from interactions across many code parts, nor to ambiguous task specifications. Without code execution, models (esp. GPT-3.5/GPT-4) tend to be overconfident in their own initial predictions and gains shrink (e.g. GPT-4 only +~3.6% on MBPP without unit-test execution). On Spider, simple correctness-only feedback without explanation barely helps. Author preliminary results: model-generated semantic-error messages add no benefit beyond line-by-line explanation.
oracle_or_external_feedback_dependency: external-tool/verifier (mixed with self-verify). The largest, most reliable gains require code execution / unit-test execution as the feedback source (TransCoder, MBPP). In the no-execution setting (Spider, and ablations on TransCoder/MBPP without execution) the method relies on intrinsic self-verification via explanation, which yields much smaller, model-dependent gains and can even hurt (e.g. Codex MBPP simple feedback without execution 61.4 -> 57.6). The ablation explicitly concludes that leveraging code execution is crucial for the performance leap. Note: it does NOT use ground-truth labels — unit tests are part of the problem spec, and Spider has no tests.
self_correction_efficacy: task-dependent / strongest with execution feedback. Net-positive when grounded by code execution/unit tests (up to +12%). When relying purely on intrinsic self-verification (no execution), gains are small and inconsistent and can be net-negative (e.g. simple feedback degrades Codex MBPP from 61.4 to 57.6); code explanation/trace recovers and modestly improves it. Demonstrates that self-correction works for code largely because of verifiable execution feedback, not pure intrinsic reflection.
calibration_effect: mixed/degrades in the no-feedback regime — the paper reports that without unit-test execution, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 tend to be overconfident in their own initial predictions, limiting self-debugging gains. Formal calibration metrics are not measured; this is a qualitative observation.
failure_attribution_capability: n/a — this is a self-correction/repair method, not a failure-attribution study. It localizes and fixes implementation errors in its own code (via explanation/trace) but does not classify failure modes via a taxonomy or attribute blame across agents/steps in the MAST sense.
failure_mode_addressed: Targets implementation bugs in self-generated code: small mistakes in otherwise-near-correct programs (e.g. missing WHERE conditions or SELECT columns in SQL; integer-vs-float division and similar semantic translation errors in C++-to-Python). It mitigates 'one-shot generation' errors and over-reliance on a single forward pass. Relative to MAST-style modes it most directly addresses superficial/incomplete reasoning and unverified outputs; it can be undermined by overconfident superficial self-reflection when no execution feedback is available.
dataset_or_benchmark_released: n/a — no new dataset or benchmark released; all experiments use existing public benchmarks (Spider, TransCoder, MBPP). The paper releases prompts in the appendix; no separate trace dataset.
builds_on: Program repair / code-fixing with feedback (Chen et al. 2023a 'Teaching LMs to self-debug via human feedback', Austin et al. 2021); execution-based candidate selection and reranking (MBR-Exec / Shi et al. 2022, Coder-Reviewer / Zhang et al. 2022, LEVER / Ni et al. 2023, Self-consistency / Wang et al. 2023); chain-of-thought and intermediate-reasoning prompting (Wei et al. 2022, Kojima et al. 2022, least-to-most Zhou et al. 2023); self-critique/self-improvement work (Self-Refine / Madaan et al. 2023, Reflexion / Shinn et al. 2023, Constitutional AI / Bai et al. 2022, self-verification / Weng et al. 2022). Rubber-duck-debugging concept (Hunt & Thomas 2000).
extended_by_or_inspired: Widely cited as a foundational training-free code self-correction baseline. Direct successors/extensions include LDB (Large Language Model Debugger, Zhong et al. 2024, runtime-state debugging), Reflexion-style verbal RL for agents (concurrent), 'Revisit Self-Debugging with Self-Generated Tests' (Chen et al. 2025, arXiv:2501.12793, post-execution vs in-execution paradigms), NExT (Ni et al. 2024, teaching execution reasoning), and weight-internalizing successors such as ReflexiCoder (Jiang et al. 2026, RL-internalized reflect-and-correct). Also informs critiques of intrinsic self-correction (Huang et al., Kamoi et al.) which emphasize its reliance on external/oracle feedback.
on_policy_distillation_link: Low/indirect. Self-Debugging is purely in-context (no distillation, no weight update, no on-policy rollouts). It is conceptually a precursor to later work that distills execution-grounded reflect-and-correct trajectories into weights via RL/SFT (e.g. NExT self-training on execution-aware rationales; ReflexiCoder RL-internalized self-correction), but the method itself has no on-policy distillation component.
sample_efficiency: High / a central claim. Applying Self-Debugging to a greedy (1-sample) prediction on Spider matches the multi-sample baseline that uses 16 samples; from 8 initial samples it outperforms the baseline using 32 samples. Overall it matches or beats baselines that generate >10x more candidate programs, with successful debugging usually completing in <=3 turns (often 1).
